entries.e0f8a51edbf26e55b256e8cf5960b054df28950c: <div sID="gen16214" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="34" osisID="Isa.34" sID="Isa.34"/> <div eID="gen16214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16215" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16216" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have the fatal doom of all the nations that are enemies to God's church and people, though Edom only is mentioned, because of the old enmity of Esau to Jacob, which was typical, as much as that more ancient enmity of Cain to Abel, and flowed from the original enmity of the serpent to the seed of the woman. It is probable that this prophecy had its accomplishment in the great desolations made by the Assyrian army first, or rather by Nebuchadnezzar's army some time after, among those nations that were neighbours to Israel and had been in some way or other injurious to them. That mighty conqueror took a pride in shedding blood, and laying countries waste, and therein, quite beyond his design, he was fulfilling what God here threatened against his and his people's enemies. But we have reason to think it is intended as a denunciation of the wrath of God against all those who fight against the interests of his kingdom among men, that it has its frequent accomplishment in the havoc made by the wars of the nations and other desolating judgments, and will have its full accomplishment in the final dissolution of all things at the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men. Here is, I. A demand of universal attention, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. A direful scene of blood and confusion presented, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.2-Isa.34.7">ver. 2-7</reference>. III. The reason given for these judgments, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.8">ver. 8</reference>. IV. The continuance of this desolation, the country being made like the lake of Sodom (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.9-Isa.34.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>), and the cities abandoned to wild beasts and melancholy fowls, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11-Isa.34.15">ver. 11-15</reference>. V. The solemn ratification of all this, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.16-Isa.34.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. Let us hear, and fear.
entries.e8719d99473234c5c3c88a2de63ae628eeef061a: <div eID="gen16216" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16215" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings against God's Enemies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen16217" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Come near, ye nations, to hear; and hearken, ye people: let the earth hear, and all that is therein; the world, and all things that come forth of it. <hi type="super">2</hi> For the indignation of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon all nations, and <hi type="italic">his</hi> fury upon all their armies: he hath utterly destroyed them, he hath delivered them to the slaughter. <hi type="super">3</hi> Their slain also shall be cast out, and their stink shall come up out of their carcases, and the mountains shall be melted with their blood. <hi type="super">4</hi> And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falleth off from the vine, and as a falling <hi type="italic">fig</hi> from the fig tree. <hi type="super">5</hi> For my sword shall be bathed in heaven: behold, it shall come down upon Idumea, and upon the people of my curse, to judgment. <hi type="super">6</hi> The sword of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is filled with blood, it is made fat with fatness, <hi type="italic">and</hi> with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the unicorns shall come down with them, and the bullocks with the bulls; and their land shall be soaked with blood, and their dust made fat with fatness. <hi type="super">8</hi> For <hi type="italic">it is</hi> the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's vengeance, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion. <div eID="gen16217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16218" type="x-p"/> Here we have a prophecy, as elsewhere we have a history, of the wars of the Lord, which we are sure are all both righteous and successful. This world, as it is his creature, he does good to; but as it is in the interest of Satan, who is called <hi type="italic">the god of this world,</hi> he fights against it. <div eID="gen16218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16219" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the trumpet sounded and the war proclaimed, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.1">v. 1</reference>. All nations must hear and hearken, not only because what God is about to do is well worthy their remark (as <reference osisRef="Isa.33.13">ch. xxxiii. 13</reference>), but because they are all concerned in it; it is with them that God has a quarrel; it is against them that God is coming forth in wrath. Let them all take notice that the great God is angry with them; his indignation is upon all nations, and therefore let all nations come near to hear. <hi type="italic">The trumpet is blown in the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.6">Amos iii. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">and the watchmen on the walls cry, Hearken to the sound of the trumpet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">Jer. vi. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Let the earth hear, and the fulness thereof, for it is the Lord's</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">Ps. xxiv. 1</reference>) and ought to hearken to its Maker and Master. The world must hear, and <hi type="italic">all things that come forth of it,</hi> the children of men, that are of the earth earthy, come out of it, and must return to it; or the inanimate products of the earth are called to, as more likely to hearken than sinners, whose hearts are hardened against the calls of God. <hi type="italic">Hear, O you mountains! the Lord's controversy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.6.2">Micah vi. 2</reference>. It is so just a controversy that all the world may be safely appealed to concerning the equity of it. <div eID="gen16219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16220" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the manifesto published, setting forth, <div eID="gen16220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16221" type="x-p"/> 1. Whom he makes war against (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">The indignation of the Lord is upon all nations;</hi> they are all in confederacy against God and religion, all in the interests of the devil, and therefore he is angry with them all, even with all the nations that forget him. He has long <hi type="italic">suffered all nations to walk in their own ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.16">Acts xiv. 16</reference>), but now he will no longer keep silence. As they have all had the benefit of his patience, so they must all expect now to feel his resentments. <hi type="italic">His fury is</hi> in a special manner <hi type="italic">upon all their armies,</hi> (1.) Because with them they have done mischief to the people of God; those are they that have made bloody work with them, and therefore they must be sure to have blood given them to drink. (2.) Because with them they hope to make their part good against the justice and power of God they trust to them as their defence, and therefore on them, in the first place, God's fury will come. Armies before God's fury are but as dry stubble before a consuming fire, though ever so numerous and courageous. <div eID="gen16221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16222" type="x-p"/> 2. Whom he makes war for, and what are the grounds and reasons of the war (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">It is the day of the Lord's vengeance,</hi> and he it is <hi type="italic">to whom vengeance belongs,</hi> and who is never <hi type="italic">unrighteous in taking vengeance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.3.5">Rom. iii. 5</reference>. As there is a day of the Lord's patience, so there will be a day of his vengeance; for, though he bear long, he will not bear always. It is <hi type="italic">the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion.</hi> Zion is the holy city, the city of our solemnities, a type and figure of the church of God in the world. Zion has a just quarrel with her neighbours for the wrongs they have done her, for all their treacherous and barbarous usage of her, profaning her holy things, laying waste her palaces, and slaying her sons. She has left it to God to plead her cause, and he will do so when the time, even the set time, to favour Zion shall have come; then he will recompense to her persecutors and oppressors all the mischiefs they have done her. The controversy will be decided, that Zion has been wronged, and therein Zion's God has been himself abused. Judgment will be given upon this decision, and execution done. Note, There is a time prefixed in the divine counsels for the deliverance of the church and the destruction of her enemies, a year of the redeemed, which will come, <hi type="italic">a year of recompences for the controversy of Zion;</hi> and we must patiently wait till then, and <hi type="italic">judge nothing before the time.</hi> <div eID="gen16222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16223" type="x-p"/> III. Here are the operations of the war, and the methods of it, settled, with an infallible assurance of success. 1. The sword of the Lord is <hi type="italic">bathed in heaven;</hi> this is all the preparation here made for the war, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.5">v. 5</reference>. It may probably allude to some custom they had then of bathing their swords in some liquor or other, to harden them or brighten them; it is the same with the furbishing of it, that it may glitter, <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.9-Ezek.21.11">Ezek. xxi. 9-11</reference>. God's sword is bathed in heaven, in his counsel and decree, in his justice and power, and then there is not standing before it. 2. <hi type="italic">It shall come down.</hi> What he has determined shall without fail be put in execution. It shall come down from heaven, and the higher the place is, whence it comes, the heavier will it fall. It will come down <hi type="italic">upon Idumea, the people of God's curse,</hi> the people that lie under his curse and are by it doomed to destruction. Miserable, for ever miserable, are those that have by their sins made themselves the people of God's curse; for the sword of the Lord will infallibly attend the curse of the Lord and execute the sentences of it; and those whom he curses are cursed indeed. It shall come down <hi type="italic">to judgment,</hi> to execute judgment upon sinners. Note, God's sword of war is always a sword of justice. It is observed of him out of whose mouth goeth the sharp sword that <hi type="italic">in righteousness he doth judge and make war,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11">Rev. xix. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.15">15</reference>. 3. The nations and their armies shall be given up to the sword (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">God has delivered them to the slaughter,</hi> and then they cannot deliver themselves, nor can all the friends they have deliver them from it. Those only are slain whom God delivers to the slaughter, for the keys of death are in his hand; and, in delivering them to the slaughter, he has <hi type="italic">utterly destroyed</hi> them; their destruction is as sure, when God has doomed them to it, as if they were destroyed already, utterly destroyed. God has, in effect, delivered all the cruel enemies of his church to the slaughter by that word (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">He that kills with the sword must be killed by the sword,</hi> for the Lord is righteous. 4. Pursuant to the sentence, a terrible slaughter shall be made among them (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sword of the Lord,</hi> when it comes down with commission, does vast execution; it <hi type="italic">is filled,</hi> satiated, surfeited, <hi type="italic">with blood,</hi> the blood of the slain, and <hi type="italic">made fat with their fatness.</hi> When the day of God's abused mercy and patience is over the sword of his justice gives no quarter, spares none. Men have by sin lost the honour of the human nature and made themselves like the beasts that perish; they are therefore justly denied the compassion and respect that are owing to the human nature and killed as beasts, and no more is made of slaying an army of men than of butchering a flock of lambs or goats and feeding on the fat of the kidneys of rams. Nay, the sword of the Lord shall not only dispatch the lambs and goats, the infantry of their armies, the poor common soldiers, but (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.7">v. 7</reference>) <hi type="italic">the unicorns</hi> too <hi type="italic">shall</hi> be made to <hi type="italic">come down with them, and the bullocks with the bulls,</hi> though they are ever so proud, and strong, and fierce (<hi type="italic">the great men, and the mighty men, and the chief captains</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev. vi. 15</reference>), the sword of the Lord will make as easy a prey of as of the lambs and the goats. The greatest of men are nothing before the wrath of the great God. See what bloody work will be made: <hi type="italic">The land shall be soaked with blood,</hi> as with the rain that comes often upon it and in great abundance; <hi type="italic">and their dust,</hi> their dry and barren land, shall be <hi type="italic">made fat with the fatness</hi> of men slain in their full strength, as with manure. Nay even <hi type="italic">the mountains,</hi> which are hard and rocky, <hi type="italic">shall be melted with their blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.34.3">v. 3</reference>. These expressions are hyperbolical (as St. John's vision of <hi type="italic">blood to the horse-bridles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.20">Rev. xiv. 20</reference>), and are made use of because they sound very dreadful to sense (it makes us even shiver to think of such abundance of human gore), and are therefore proper to express the terror of God's wrath, which is dreadful beyond conception and expression. See what work sin and wrath make even in this world, and think how much more terrible the wrath to come is, which will bring down the unicorns themselves to the bars of the pit. 5. This great slaughter will be a great sacrifice to the justice of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has a sacrifice in Bozrah;</hi> there it is that the great Redeemer has his <hi type="italic">garments dyed with blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">ch. lxiii. 1</reference>. Sacrifices were intended for the honour of God, to make it appear that he hates sin and demands satisfaction for it, and that nothing but blood will make atonement; and for these ends the slaughter is made, that in it <hi type="italic">the wrath of God may be revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men,</hi> especially their ungodly unrighteous enmity to his people, which was the sin that the Edomites were notoriously guilty of. In great sacrifices abundance of beasts were killed, hecatombs offered, and their blood poured out before the altar; and so will it be in this day of the Lord's vengeance. And thus would the whole earth have been soaked with the blood of sinners if Jesus Christ, the great propitiation, had not shed his blood for us; but those who reject him, and will not make a covenant with God by that sacrifice, will themselves fall as victims to divine wrath. Damned sinners are everlasting sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Mark.9.48-Mark.9.49">Mark ix. 48, 49</reference>. Those that sacrifice not (which is the character of the ungodly, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2">Eccl. ix. 2</reference>) must be sacrificed. 6. These slain shall be detestable to mankind, and shall be as much their loathing as ever they were their terror (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall be cast out,</hi> and none shall pay them the respect of a decent burial; but <hi type="italic">their stink shall come up out of their carcases,</hi> that all people by the odious smell, as well as by the ghastly sight, may be made to conceive an indignation against sin and a dread of the wrath of God. They lie unburied, that they may remain monuments of divine justice. 7. The effect and consequence of this slaughter shall be universal confusion and desolation, as if the whole frame of nature were dissolved and melted down (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">All the host of heaven shall pine and waste away</hi> (so the word is); the sun shall be darkened, and the moon look black, or be turned into blood; <hi type="italic">the heavens</hi> themselves <hi type="italic">shall be rolled together as a scroll</hi> or parchment when we have done with it, and lay it by, or as when it is shrivelled up by the heat of the fire. The stars shall fall as the leaves in autumn; all the beauty, joy, and comfort, of the vanquished nation shall be lost and done away, magistracy and government shall be abolished, and all dominion and rule, but that of the sword of war, shall fall. Conquerors, in those times, affected to lay waste the countries they conquered; and such a complete desolation is here described by such figurative expressions as will yet have a literal and full accomplishment in the dissolution of all things at the end of time, of which last day of judgment the judgments which God does now sometimes remarkably execute on sinful nations are figures, earnests, and forerunners; and by these we should be awakened to think of that, for which reason these expressions are used here and <reference osisRef="Rev.6.12-Rev.6.13">Rev. vi. 12, 13</reference>. But they are used without a metaphor, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2 Pet. iii. 10</reference>, where we are told that <hi type="italic">the heavens shall pass away with a great noise and the earth shall be burnt up.</hi>
entries.bab460a5467fa5735843e1ce89ebeb1ab3c53d30: <div eID="gen16223" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings against God's Enemies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen16224" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And the streams thereof shall be turned into pitch, and the dust thereof into brimstone, and the land thereof shall become burning pitch. <hi type="super">10</hi> It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever. <hi type="super">11</hi> But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness. <hi type="super">12</hi> They shall call the nobles thereof to the kingdom, but none <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> there, and all her princes shall be nothing. <hi type="super">13</hi> And thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof: and it shall be a habitation of dragons, <hi type="italic">and</hi> a court for owls. <hi type="super">14</hi> The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; the screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest. <hi type="super">15</hi> There shall the great owl make her nest, and lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow: there shall the vultures also be gathered, every one with her mate. <hi type="super">16</hi> Seek ye out of the book of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and read: no one of these shall fail, none shall want her mate: for my mouth it hath commanded, and his spirit it hath gathered them. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he hath cast the lot for them, and his hand hath divided it unto them by line: they shall possess it for ever, from generation to generation shall they dwell therein. <div eID="gen16224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16225" type="x-p"/> This prophecy looks very black, but surely it looks so further than upon Edom and Bozrah. 1. It describes the melancholy changes that are often made by the divine Providence, in countries, cities, palaces, and families. Places that have flourished and been much frequented strangely go to decay. We know not where to find the places where many great towns, celebrated in history, once stood. Fruitful countries, in process of time, are turned into barrenness, and pompous populous cities into ruinous heaps. Old decayed castles look frightful, and their ruins are almost as much dreaded as ever their garrisons were. 2. It describes the destroying judgments which are the effects of God's wrath and the just punishment of those that are enemies to his people, which God will inflict when <hi type="italic">the year of the redeemed has come,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion.</hi> Those that aim to ruin the church can never do that, but will infallibly ruin themselves. 3. It describes the final desolation of this wicked world, which is <hi type="italic">reserved unto fire at the day of judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.7">2 Pet. iii. 7</reference>. The earth itself, when it, and all the works that are therein, shall be burnt up, will (for aught I know) be turned into a hell to all those that set their affections on earthly things. However, this prophecy shows us what will be the lot of the <hi type="italic">generation of God's curse.</hi> <div eID="gen16225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16226" type="x-p"/> I. The country shall become like the lake of Sodom, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.9-Isa.34.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">The streams thereof,</hi> that both watered the land and pleased and refreshed the inhabitants, <hi type="italic">shall</hi> now <hi type="italic">be turned into pitch,</hi> shall be congealed, shall look black, and shall move slowly, or not at all. <hi type="italic">Their floods to lazy streams of pitch shall turn;</hi> so Sir <hi type="italic">R. Blackmore. The dust thereof shall be turned into brimstone;</hi> so combustible has sin made their land that it shall take fire at the first spark of God's wrath struck upon it; and, when it has taken fire, it shall become burning pitch; the fire shall be universal, not a house, or town, on fire, but a whole country; and it shall not be in the power of any to suppress or extinguish it. It shall burn continually, burn perpetually, and <hi type="italic">shall not be quenched night nor day.</hi> The torment of those in hell, or that have a hell within them in their own consciences, is without interruption; the <hi type="italic">smoke of this fire goes up for ever.</hi> As long as there are provoking sinners on earth, <hi type="italic">from one generation to another,</hi> an increase of sinful men, to <hi type="italic">augment the fierce anger of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.32.14">Num. xxxii. 14</reference>), there will be a righteous God in heaven to punish them for it. And as long as a people keep up a succession of sinners God will have a succession of plagues for them; nor will any that fall under the wrath of God be ever able to recover themselves. It will be found, how light soever men make of it, that it is a <hi type="italic">fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.</hi> If the land be doomed to destruction, none shall pass through it, but travellers will choose rather to go a great way about than come within the smell of it. <div eID="gen16226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16227" type="x-p"/> II. The cities shall become like old decayed houses, which, being deserted by the owners, look very frightful, being commonly possessed by beasts of prey or birds of ill omen. See how dismally the palaces of the enemy look; the description is peculiarly elegant and fine. 1. God shall mark them for ruin and destruction. <hi type="italic">He shall stretch out upon Bozrah the line of confusion with the stones</hi> or plummets <hi type="italic">of emptiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">v. 11</reference>. This intimates the equity of the sentence passed upon it; it is given according to the rules of justice and the exact agreeableness of the execution with the sentence; the destruction is not wrought at random, but by line and level. The confusion and emptiness that shall overspread the face of the whole country shall be like that of the whole earth when it was <hi type="italic">Tohu and Bohu</hi> (the very words here used)—<hi type="italic">without form and void.</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen. i. 2</reference>. Sin will soon turn a paradise into a chaos, and sully the beauty of the whole creation. When there is confusion there will soon be emptiness; but both are appointed by the governor of the world, and in exact proportions. 2. Their great men shall be all cut off, and none of them shall dare to appear (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall call the nobles of the kingdom</hi> to take care of the arduous affairs which lie before them, but none shall be there to take this ruin under their hand, and all her princes, having the sad tidings brought them, shall be nothing, shall be at their wits' end, and not be able to stand them in stead, to shelter them from destruction. <div eID="gen16227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16228" type="x-p"/> III. Even the houses of state, and those of strength, shall become as wildernesses (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.13">v. 13</reference>); not only grass shall grow, but <hi type="italic">thorns shall come up, in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof,</hi> and there shall be none to cut them up or tread them down. We sometimes see ruined buildings thus overgrown with rubbish. It intimates that the place shall not only be uninhabited and unfrequented where a full court used to be kept, but that it shall be under the curse of God; for thorns and thistles were the production of the curse, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.18">Gen. iii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen16228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16229" type="x-p"/> IV. They shall become the residence and rendezvous of fearful frightful beasts and birds, which usually frequent such melancholy places, because there they may be undisturbed, and, when they are frightened thither, they help to frighten men thence. This circumstance of the desolation, being apt to strike a horror upon the mind, is much enlarged upon here, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">The cormorant shall possess it,</hi> or the pelican, which affects to be solitary (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.6">Ps. cii. 6</reference>); and <hi type="italic">the bittern,</hi> which makes a hideous noise, <hi type="italic">the owl,</hi> a melancholy bird, <hi type="italic">the raven,</hi> a bird of prey, invited by the dead carcases, shall dwell there (<hi type="italic">with all the ill-boding monsters of the air,</hi> Sir <hi type="italic">R. B.</hi>), all the unclean birds, which were not for the service of man, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">It shall be a habitation for dragons,</hi> which are poisonous and hurtful. <div eID="gen16229" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen16230"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16231"/>And in their lofty rooms of state,<l eID="gen16231" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16232"/>Where cringing sycophants did wait,<l eID="gen16232" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16233"/>Dragons shall hiss and hungry wolves shall howl;<l eID="gen16233" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16234"/>In courts before by mighty lords possess'd<l eID="gen16234" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16235"/>The serpent shall erect his speckled crest,<l eID="gen16235" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16236"/>Or fold his circling spires to rest. <hi type="small-caps">Sir R. Blackmore</hi> .<l eID="gen16236" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen16230"/> <div sID="gen16237" type="x-p"/> That which was a court for princes shall now be a court for owls or ostriches, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">The wild beasts of the desert,</hi> the dry and sandy country, shall meet, as it were by appointment, with the wild beasts of the island, the wet marshy country, and shall regale themselves with such a perfect desolation as they shall find there. <div eID="gen16237" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen16238"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16239"/>Leopards, and all the rav'ning brotherhoods<l eID="gen16239" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16240"/>That range the plains, or lurk in woods,<l eID="gen16240" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16241"/>Each other shall invite to come,<l eID="gen16241" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16242"/>And make this wilder place their home.<l eID="gen16242" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16243"/>Fierce beasts of every frightful shape and size<l eID="gen16243" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16244"/>Shall settle here their bloody colonies. <hi type="small-caps">Sir R. Blackmore</hi> .<l eID="gen16244" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen16238"/> <div sID="gen16245" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">The satyr shall cry to his fellow</hi> to go with him to this desert place, or, being there, they shall please themselves that they have found such an agreeable habitation. There shall <hi type="italic">the screech-owl rest,</hi> a night-bird and an ominous one. <hi type="italic">The great owl shall there make her nest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.15">v. 15</reference>) <hi type="italic">and lay and hatch;</hi> the breed of them shall be kept up to provide heirs for this desolate place. <hi type="italic">The vultures</hi> which feast on carcases, <hi type="italic">shall be gathered there, every one with his mate.</hi> Now observe, 1. How the places which men have deserted, and keep at a distance from, are proper receptacles for other animals, which the providence of God takes care of, and will not neglect. 2. Whom those resemble that are morose, unsociable, and unconversable, and affect a melancholy retirement; they are like these solitary creatures that take delight in desolations. 3. What a dismal change sin makes; it turns a fruitful land into barrenness, a frequented city into a wilderness. <div eID="gen16245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16246" type="x-p"/> V. Here is an assurance given of the full accomplishment of this prediction, even to the most minute circumstance of it (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.16-Isa.34.17">v. 16, 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Seek you out of the book of the Lord and read.</hi> When this destruction comes compare the event with the prediction, and you will find it to answer exactly." Note, The book of the prophets is the book of the Lord, and we ought to consult it and converse with it as of divine origin and authority. We must not only read it, but see out of it, search into it, turn first to one text and then to another and compare them together. Abundance of useful knowledge might thus be extracted, by a diligent search, out of the scriptures, which cannot be got by a superficial reading of them. When you have read the prediction out of the book of the Lord then observe, 1. That according to what you have read so you see; <hi type="italic">not one of these shall fail,</hi> either beast or fowl: and, it being foretold that they shall possess it <hi type="italic">from generation to generation,</hi> in order to that, that the species may be propagated, <hi type="italic">none shall want her mate;</hi> these marks of desolation shall be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the land. 2. That God's mouth having commanded this direful muster <hi type="italic">his Spirit shall gather them,</hi> as the creatures by instinct were gathered to Adam to be named and to Noah to be housed. What God's word has appointed his Spirit will effect and bring about, for no word of God shall fall to the ground. The word of God's promise shall in like manner be accomplished by the operations of the Spirit. 3. That there is an exact order and proportion observed in the accomplishment of this threatening: <hi type="italic">He has cast the lot</hi> for these birds and beasts, so that each one shall know his place as readily as if it were marked by line. See the like, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.7-Joel.2.8">Joel ii. 7, 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">They shall not break their ranks, neither shall one thrust another.</hi> The soothsayers among the heathen foretold events by the flight of birds, as if the fate of men depended on them. But here we find that the flight of birds is under the direction of the God of Israel: <hi type="italic">he has cast the lot for them.</hi> 4. That the desolation shall be perpetual: <hi type="italic">They shall possess it for ever.</hi> God's Jerusalem may be laid in ruins; but Jerusalem of old recovered itself out of its ruins, till it gave place to the gospel Jerusalem, which may be brought low, but shall be rebuilt, and shall continue till it give place to the heavenly Jerusalem. But the enemies of the church shall be for ever desolate, shall be punished with an everlasting destruction.  <chapter eID="Isa.34"/> <div eID="gen16246" type="x-p"/>

entries.00bede7c8b03da417997e380ead6790a38241379: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8939"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 34</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.34.1-Isa.34.17">Is 34:1-17</reference>. Judgment on Idumea.</title> <div sID="gen15003" type="x-p"/> The thirty-fourth and thirty-fifth chapters form one prophecy, the former part of which denounces God's judgment against His people's enemies, of whom Edom is the representative; the second part, of the flourishing state of the Church consequent on those judgments. This forms the termination of the prophecies of the first part of Isaiah (the thirty-sixth through thirty-ninth chapters being historical) and is a kind of summary of what went before, setting forth the one main truth, Israel shall be delivered from all its foes, and happier times shall succeed under Messiah.<div eID="gen15003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15004" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8939"/>1. All creation is summoned to hear God's judgments (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.3">Eze 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.1">De 32:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.4">Psa 50:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.1">Mi 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2</reference>), for they set forth His glory, which is the end of creation (<reference osisRef="Rev.15.3">Re 15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.4.11">4:11</reference>).<div eID="gen15004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that come forth of it--</hi>answering to "all that is therein"; or Hebrew, "all whatever fills it," Margin. <div eID="gen15005" type="x-p"/>
entries.d26becfcf6203a6da41aa3af06da51637377a29d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8940"/><div sID="gen15006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8940"/><hi type="bold">2. utterly destroyed--</hi>rather, "doomed them to an utter curse" [Horsley].<div eID="gen15006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered--</hi>rather, "appointed." <div eID="gen15007" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c6f7c8ba00984cd2001b1fc9d647bb0e0848ff3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8941"/><div sID="gen15008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8941"/><hi type="bold">3. cast out--</hi>unburied (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">Is 14:19</reference>).<div eID="gen15008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">melted--</hi>washed away as with a descending torrent. <div eID="gen15009" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5350f1c881187bb09c0000b26e5f22132102d99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8942"/><div sID="gen15010" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8942"/>4. (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.26">Psa 102:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.31">Joe 2:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.15">3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">Mt 24:29</reference>).<div eID="gen15010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dissolved--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10-2Pet.3.12">2Pe 3:10-12</reference>). Violent convulsions of nature are in Scripture made the images of great changes in the human world (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.19-Isa.24.21">Is 24:19-21</reference>), and shall literally accompany them at the winding up of the present dispensation.<div eID="gen15011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scroll--</hi>Books were in those days sheets of parchment rolled together (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.14">Re 6:14</reference>).<div eID="gen15012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fall down--</hi>The stars shall fall when the heavens in which they are fixed pass away.<div eID="gen15013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fig tree--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.6.13">Re 6:13</reference>). <div eID="gen15014" type="x-p"/>
entries.89883c79b30918ddccdba5f177a07b25feb1c019: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8943"/><div sID="gen15015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8943"/><hi type="bold">5. sword--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">Jr 46:10</reference>). Or else, knife for sacrifice for God does not here appear as a warrior with His sword, but as one about to sacrifice victims doomed to slaughter [Vitringa]. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.39.17">Eze 39:17</reference>).<div eID="gen15015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bathed--</hi>rather "intoxicated," namely, with anger (so <reference osisRef="Deut.32.42">De 32:42</reference>). "In heaven" implies the place where God's purpose of wrath is formed in antithesis to its "coming down" in the next clause.<div eID="gen15016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Idumea--</hi>originally extending from the Dead Sea to the Red Sea; afterwards they obtained possession of the country east of Moab, of which Bozrah was capital. Petra or Selah, called Joktheel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">2Ki 14:7</reference>), was capital of South Edom (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">Is 16:1</reference>). David subjugated Edom (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.13">2Sa 8:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">14</reference>). Under Jehoram they regained independence (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.8">2Ch 21:8</reference>). Under Amaziah they were again subdued, and Selah taken (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">2Ki 14:7</reference>). When Judah was captive in Babylon, Edom, in every way, insulted over her fallen mistress, killed many of those Jews whom the Chaldeans had left, and hence was held guilty of fratricide by God (Esau, their ancestor, having been brother to Jacob): this was the cause of the denunciations of the prophets against Edom (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Is 63:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jr 49:7</reference>; Eze 25:12-14; 35:<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3-Ezek.14.15">3-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.19">Joe 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">Am 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>; Ob 8, 10, 12-18; Mal <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.4">1:3,4</reference>). Nebuchadnezzar humbled Idumea accordingly (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.21">Jr 25:15-21</reference>).<div eID="gen15017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of my curse--</hi>that is, doomed to it.<div eID="gen15018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to judgment--</hi>that is, to execute it. <div eID="gen15019" type="x-p"/>
entries.b27ee4fb96273c8ee984e37b1ca218bc9a09be48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8944"/><div sID="gen15020" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8944"/><hi type="bold">6. filled--</hi>glutted. The image of a sacrifice is continued.<div eID="gen15020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blood ... fat--</hi>the parts especially devoted to God in a sacrifice (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.22">2Sa 1:22</reference>).<div eID="gen15021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lambs ... goats--</hi>sacrificial animals: the Idumeans, of all classes, doomed to slaughter, are meant (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.7">Zep 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen15022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bozrah--</hi>called Bostra by the Romans, &c., assigned in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.24">Jr 48:24</reference> to Moab, so that it seems to have been at one time in the dominion of Edom, and at another in that of Moab (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Is 63:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.13">Jr 49:13</reference>, 20, 22); it was strictly not in Edom, but the capital of Auranitis (the Houran). Edom seems to have extended its dominion so as to include it (compare <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">La 4:21</reference>). <div eID="gen15023" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfea95bb690aad4ca9239bce314548da2c6290c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8945"/><div sID="gen15024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8945"/><hi type="bold">7. unicorns--</hi>Hebrew, reem: conveying the idea of loftiness, power, and pre-eminence (see on <reference osisRef="Job.39.9">Job 39:9</reference>), in the Bible. At one time the image in the term answers to a reality in nature; at another it symbolizes an abstraction. The rhinoceros was the original type. The Arab rim is two-horned: it was the oryx (the leucoryx, antelope, bold and pugnacious); but when accident or artifice deprived it of one horn, the notion of the unicorn arose. Here is meant the portion of the Edomites which was strong and warlike.<div eID="gen15024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come down--</hi>rather, "fall down," slain [Lowth].<div eID="gen15025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with them--</hi>with the "lambs and goats," the less powerful Edomites (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Is 34:6</reference>).<div eID="gen15026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bullocks ... bulls--</hi>the young and old Edomites: all classes.<div eID="gen15027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dust--</hi>ground. <div eID="gen15028" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa0e2a706f7d7cb67fab393b4988df10de4590ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8946"/><div sID="gen15029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8946"/><hi type="bold">8. recompenses for the controversy of Zion--</hi>that is, the year when God will retaliate on those who have contended with Zion. Her controversy is His. Edom had thought to extend its borders by laying hold of its neighbor's lands and has instigated Babylon to cruelty towards fallen Judah (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.5">Eze 36:5</reference>); therefore Edom shall suffer the same herself (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">La 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">22</reference>). The final winding up of the controversy between God and all enemies of Him and His people is also foreshadowed (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.2">Is 61:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.4">63:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.14-Isa.66.16">66:14-16</reference>; Mal 4:1, 3; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.7">2Th 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.9">8, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.18">Re 11:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.20">18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.2">19:2</reference>). <div eID="gen15029" type="x-p"/>
entries.3db1baf8cd41a4f37c07821ad7644395b864af20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8947"/><div sID="gen15030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8947"/>9. Images from the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.24-Gen.19.28">Ge 19:24-28</reference>; so <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">De 29:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.17">Jr 49:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen15030" type="x-p"/>
entries.51b06b456c3a8018a9264b5bfae9fe1b5c149eb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8948"/><div sID="gen15031" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8948"/><hi type="bold">10. It--</hi>The burning pitch, &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.9">Is 34:9</reference>).<div eID="gen15031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smoke ... for ever--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.14.11">Re 14:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.18">18:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.3">19:3</reference>).<div eID="gen15032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">generation to generation--</hi>(Mal 1:4).<div eID="gen15033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15034" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none ... pass through--</hi>Edom's original offense was: they would not let Israel pass through their land in peace to Canaan: God recompenses them in kind, no traveller shall pass through Edom. Volney, the infidel, was forced to confirm the truth of this prophecy: "From the reports of the Arabs, southeast of the Dead Sea, within three days' journey are upwards of thirty ruined towns, absolutely deserted." <div eID="gen15034" type="x-p"/>
entries.9669d94553bed2f7c9fd1d79fba351028b591df3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8949"/><div sID="gen15035" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8949"/><hi type="bold">11. cormorant--</hi>The Hebrew is rendered, in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.6">Psa 102:6</reference>, "pelican," which is a seafowl, and cannot be meant here: some waterfowl (katta, according to Burckhardt) that tenants desert places is intended.<div eID="gen15035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bittern--</hi>rather, "the hedgehog," or "porcupine" [Gesenius] (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.23">Is 14:23</reference>).<div eID="gen15036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">owl--</hi>from its being enumerated among water birds in <reference osisRef="Lev.11.17">Le 11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.16">De 14:16</reference>. Maurer thinks rather the heron or crane is meant; from a Hebrew root, "to blow," as it utters a sound like the blowing of a horn (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Re 18:2</reference>).<div eID="gen15037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">confusion--</hi>devastation.<div eID="gen15038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">line ... stones--</hi>metaphor from an architect with line and plummet-stone (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Is 18:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Is 28:17</reference>); God will render to it the exact measure of justice without mercy (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.13">Jas 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.13">2Ki 21:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">La 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.7.7">Am 7:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen15039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">emptiness--</hi>desolation. Edom is now a waste of "stones." <div eID="gen15040" type="x-p"/>
entries.fdfda67cb9e1dc10934903e2f08522d8bb5c887e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8950"/><div sID="gen15041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8950"/>12. Rather, "As to her nobles, there shall be none there who shall declare a kingdom," that is, a king [Maurer]; or else, "There shall be no one there whom they shall call to the kingdom" [Rosenmuller] (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.6">Is 3:6</reference>, &c.). Idumea was at first governed by dukes (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.15">Ge 36:15</reference>); out of them the king wan chosen when the constitution became a monarchy. <div eID="gen15041" type="x-p"/>
entries.7479b1d512e2f89e08538bab7aa86a8f9bb55b47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8951"/><div sID="gen15042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8951"/><hi type="bold">13. dragons--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.13.21">Is 13:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">Is 13:22</reference>).<div eID="gen15042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">court for owls--</hi>rather, "a dwelling for ostriches." <div eID="gen15043" type="x-p"/>
entries.67f5de5d100b1dc5af607ed9110a5e21996f6835: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8952"/><div sID="gen15044" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8952"/><hi type="bold">14. wild beasts of the desert ... island--</hi>rather, "wild cats ... jackals" (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.21">Is 13:21</reference>).<div eID="gen15044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">screech owl--</hi>rather, "the night specter"; in Jewish superstition a female, elegantly dressed, that carried off children by night. The text does not assert the existence of such objects of superstition, but describes the place as one which superstition would people with such beings. <div eID="gen15045" type="x-p"/>
entries.f052cba986344c6075470c1bb8144a0c30704eae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8953"/><div sID="gen15046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8953"/><hi type="bold">15. great owl--</hi>rather, "the arrow snake," so called from its darting on its prey [Gesenius].<div eID="gen15046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lay--</hi>namely, eggs.<div eID="gen15047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gather under her shadow--</hi>rather, "cherishes" her young under, &c. (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.11">Jr 17:11</reference>). <div eID="gen15048" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcf9989e892abbd8e1e4af55dbae0b998153179c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8954"/><div sID="gen15049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8954"/><hi type="bold">16. book of the Lord--</hi>the volume in which the various prophecies and other parts of Scripture began henceforward to be collected together (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.8">Is 30:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">Da 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen15049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Seek--</hi>(so <reference osisRef="Isa.8.16">Is 8:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.39">Joh 5:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.52">7:52</reference>).<div eID="gen15050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no one ... fail--</hi>of these prophecies (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.18">Mt 5:18</reference>).<div eID="gen15051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none shall want ... mate--</hi>image from pairing of animals mentioned, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.15">Is 34:15</reference> ("mate"); no prediction shall want a fulfilment as its companion. entries.f737969eed1f460fe50d19d906ddffb9e5e01fc0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8955"/><div sID="gen15055" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8955"/><hi type="bold">17. cast ... lot--</hi>As conquerors apportion lands by lot, so Jehovah has appointed and marked out ("divided") Edom for the wild beasts (<reference osisRef="Num.26.55">Nu 26:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.26.56">56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.18.4-Josh.18.6">Jos 18:4-6</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.34"/>

entries.1179790fd1001b90291a5bfa0ba763345d58273d: <div eID="gen27884" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27885" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27886" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27886" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27885" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27887" type="x-p"/> The prophet earnestly exhorts all nations to attend to the communication which he has received from Jehovah, as the matter is of the highest importance, and of universal concern, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.1">Isa 34:1</reference>. The wrath of God is denounced against all the nations that had provoked to anger the Defender of the cause of Zion, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.2">Isa 34:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.3">Isa 34:3</reference>. Great crowd of images, by which the final overthrow and utter extermination of every thing that opposes the spread of true religion in the earth are forcibly and majestically set forth; images so very bold and expressive as to render it impossible, without doing great violence to symbolical language, to restrain their import to the calamities which befell the Edomites in the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, or in that of any other potentate, or even to the calamities which the enemies of the Church have yet suffered since the delivery of the prophecy. Edom must therefore be a type of Antichrist, the last grand adversary of the people of God; and consequently this most awful prophecy, in its ultimate signification, remains to be accomplished, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.4-Isa.34.15">Isa 34:4-15</reference>. The Churches of God, at the period of the consummation, commanded to consult the book of Jehovah, and note the exact fulfillment of these terrible predictions in their minutest details. Not one jot or little relative even to the circumstances shadowed forth by the impure animals shall be found to fail; for what the mouth of the Lord has declared necessary to satisfy the Divine justice, his Spirit will accomplish, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.16">Isa 34:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.17">Isa 34:17</reference>. <div eID="gen27887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27888" type="x-p"/> This and the following chapter make one distinct prophecy; an entire, regular, and beautiful poem, consisting of two parts: the first containing a denunciation of Divine vengeance against the enemies of the people or Church of God; the second describing the flourishing state of the Church of God consequent upon the execution of those judgments. The event foretold is represented as of the highest importance, and of universal concern: All nations are called upon to attend to the declaration of it; and the wrath of God is denounced against all the nations, that is, all those that had provoked to anger the Defender of the cause of Zion. Among those, Edom is particularly specified. The principal provocation of Edom was their insulting the Jews in their distress, and joining against them with their enemies, the Chaldeans; see <reference osisRef="Amo.1.11">Amo 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.25.12">Eze 25:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.35.15">Eze 35:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>. Accordingly the Edomites were, together with the rest of the neighboring nations, ravaged and laid waste by Nebuchadnezzar; see <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.26">Jer 25:15-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.1.3">Mal 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mal.1.4">Mal 1:4</reference>, and see Marsham, Can. Chron. Saec. xviii., who calls this the age of the destruction of cities. The general devastation spread through all these countries by Nebuchadnezzar may be the event which the prophet has primarily in view in the thirty-fourth chapter: but this event, as far as we have any account of it in history, seems by no means to come up to the terms of the prophecy, or to justify so highly wrought and terrible a description; and it is not easy to discover what connection the extremely flourishing state of the Church or people of God, described in the next chapter, could have with those events, and how the former could be the consequence of the latter, as it is there represented to be. By a figure, very common in the prophetical writings, any city or people, remarkably distinguished as enemies of the people and kingdom of God, is put for those enemies in general. This seems here to be the case with Edom and Botsra. It seems, therefore, reasonable to suppose, with many learned expositors, that this prophecy has a farther view to events still future; to some great revolutions to be effected in later times, antecedent to that more perfect state of the kingdom of God upon earth, and serving to introduce it, which the Holy Scriptures warrant us to expect. <div eID="gen27888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27889" type="x-p"/> That the thirty-fifth chapter has a view beyond any thing that could be the immediate consequence of those events, is plain from every part, especially from the middle of it, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.5">Isa 35:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.6">Isa 35:6</reference>; where the miraculous works wrought by our blessed Savior are so clearly specified, that we cannot avoid making the application: and our Savior himself has moreover plainly referred to this very passage, as speaking of him and his works, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.4">Mat 11:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.5">Mat 11:5</reference>. He bids the disciples of John to go and report to their master the things which they heard and saw; that the blind received their sight, the lame walked, and the deaf heard; and leaves it to him to draw the conclusion in answer to his inquiry, whether he who performed the very works which the prophets foretold should be performed by the Messiah, was not indeed the Messiah himself. And where are these works so distinctly marked by any of the prophets as in this place? and how could they be marked more distinctly? To these the strictly literal interpretation of the prophet's words directs us. According to the allegorical interpretation they may have a farther view: this part of the prophecy may run parallel with the former and relate to the future advent of Christ; to the conversion of the Jews, and their restitution to their land; to the extension and purification of the Christian faith; events predicted in the Holy Scriptures as preparatory to it. Kimchi says, "This chapter points out the future destruction of Rome, which is here called Bosra; for Bosra was a great city of the Edomites. Now the major part of the Romans are Edomites, who profess the law of Jesus. The Emperor Caesar (qy. Constantine) was an Edomite, and so were all the emperors after him. The destruction of the Turkish empire is also comprehended in this prophecy." - L. As to the last, I say, Amen! <div eID="gen27889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27890" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27891" type="x-p"/> Hearken "Attend unto me" - A MS. adds in this line the word אלי ali, unto me, after לאמים leummim; which seems to be genuine.
entries.73b2044601b4a73518dc65902e524f332f53cd85: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27892" type="x-p"/> And all the host of heaven See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.24.21">Isa 24:21</reference>, and De Sacra Poesi Hebraeorum, Prael. ix.
entries.fa6d9443b0ae290f1a47406b372313a5735caf89: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27893" type="x-p"/> For my sword shall be bathed in heaven "For my sword is made bare in the heavens" - There seems to be some impropriety in this, according to the present reading: "My sword is made drunken, or is bathed in the heavens; "which forestalls, and expresses not in its proper place, what belongs to the next verse: for the sword of Jehovah was not to be bathed or glutted with blood in the heavens, but in Botsra and the land of Edom. In the heavens it was only prepared for slaughter. To remedy this, Archbishop Secker proposes to read, for בשמים bashshamayim, בדמם bedamim; referring to <reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">Jer 46:10</reference>. But even this is premature, and not in its proper place. The Chaldee, for רותה rivvethah, has תתגלי tithgalli, shall be revealed or disclosed: perhaps he read תראה teraeh or נראתה nirathah. Whatever reading, different I presume from the present, he might find in his copy, I follow the sense which he has given of it.
entries.c7f33817fcf09b73610bac8e2e48c9e63411a120: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27894" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath a sacrifice "For Jehovah celebrateth a sacrifice" - Ezekiel, <reference osisRef="Eze.39.16">Eze 39:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.39.17">Eze 39:17</reference>, has manifestly imitated this place of Isaiah. He hath set forth the great leaders and princes of the adverse powers under the same emblems of goats, bulls, rams, fatlings, etc., and has added to the boldness of the imagery, by introducing God as summoning all the fowls of the air, and all the beasts of the field, and bidding them to the feast which he has prepared for them by the slaughter of the enemies of his people: - "And thou, son of man, <div eID="gen27894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27895" type="x-p"/> Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, <div eID="gen27895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27896" type="x-p"/> Say to the bird of every wing, <div eID="gen27896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27897" type="x-p"/> And to every beast of the field: <div eID="gen27897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27898" type="x-p"/> Assemble yourselves, and come; <div eID="gen27898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27899" type="x-p"/> Gather together from every side, <div eID="gen27899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27900" type="x-p"/> To the sacrifice which I make for you, <div eID="gen27900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27901" type="x-p"/> A great slaughter on the mountains of Israel. <div eID="gen27901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27902" type="x-p"/> And ye shall eat flesh and drink blood: <div eID="gen27902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27903" type="x-p"/> The flesh of the mighty shall ye eat, <div eID="gen27903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27904" type="x-p"/> And the blood of the lofty of the earth shall ye drink; <div eID="gen27904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27905" type="x-p"/> Of rams, of lambs, and of goats, <div eID="gen27905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27906" type="x-p"/> Of bullocks, all of them the fat ones of Bashan; <div eID="gen27906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27907" type="x-p"/> And ye shall eat fat, till ye are cloyed, <div eID="gen27907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27908" type="x-p"/> And drink blood, till ye are drunken; <div eID="gen27908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27909" type="x-p"/> Of my slaughter, which I have slain for you." <div eID="gen27909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27910" type="x-p"/> The sublime author of the <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17">Rev 19:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.18">Rev 19:18</reference>, has taken this image from Ezekiel, rather than from Isaiah.
entries.3a948916301ce5190a0f0badbf2518fa834ffba1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27911" type="x-p"/> The unicorns shall come down - ראמים reemim, translated wild goats by Bishop Lowth. The ראם reem Bochart thinks to be a species of wild goat in the deserts of Arabia. It seems generally to mean the rhinoceros. <div eID="gen27911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27912" type="x-p"/> With blood "With their blood" - מדמם middamam; so two ancient MSS. of Kennicott's the Syriac, and Chaldee.
entries.cb07d373ccfe17ad98bcd1f929429cf682d1409a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27913" type="x-p"/> The year of recompenses for the controversy of Zion "The year of recompense to the defender of the cause of Zion" - As from דון dun, דין din, a judge; so from רוב rub, ריב rib, an advocate, or defender; Judici Sionis: Syriac.
entries.2e9241c8a1463d81fe63284d3211ae1791e05cd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27914" type="x-p"/> The cormorant - קאת kaath, the pelican, from the root קיא ki, to vomit, because it is said she swallows shell-fish, and when the heat of her stomach has killed the fish, she vomits the shells, takes out the dead fish, and eats them. <div eID="gen27914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27915" type="x-p"/> The bittern - קפד kippod, the hedge-hog, or porcupine. <div eID="gen27915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27916" type="x-p"/> The owl - ינשוף yanshoph, the bittern, from נשף nashaph, to blow, because of the blowing noise it makes, almost like the lowing of an ox. My old MS. Bible renders the words thus: - The foule in face like an asse, and the yrchoun, and the snyte (snipe.) <div eID="gen27916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27917" type="x-p"/> The line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness "The plummet of emptiness over her scorched plains" - The word חריה choreyha, joined to the 12th verse, embarrasses it, and makes it inexplicable. At least I do not know that any one has yet made out the construction, or given any tolerable explication of it. I join it to the 11th verse, and supply a letter or two, which seem to have been lost. Fifteen MSS. five ancient, and two editions, read חוריה choreyha; the first printed edition of 1486, I think nearer to the truth, חור חריה chor choreyha. I read בחרריה becharereyha, or על חרריה al chorereyha; see <reference osisRef="Jer.17.6">Jer 17:6</reference>. A MS. has חדיה chodiah, and the Syriac reads חדוה chaduah, gaudium, joining it to the two preceding words; which he likewise reads differently, but without improving the sense. However, his authority is clear for dividing the verses as they are here divided. I read שם shem, as a noun. They shall boast, יקראו yikreu; see <reference osisRef="Pro.20.6">Pro 20:6</reference>.
entries.5a907b7440ec071ed752562e974b67dc069d7be5: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen27917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27918" type="x-p"/> And thorns shall come up in her palaces - ועלו בארמנותיה vealu bearmenotheyha; so read all the ancient versions. <div eID="gen27918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27919" type="x-p"/> A court for owls - יענה yaanah, the ostrich, from ענה anah, to cry, because of the noise it makes. "They roar, "says Dr. Shaw, "sometimes like a lion - sometimes like a bull. I have often heard them groan as if in the utmost distress."
entries.0c78078a14ccbc5a6ce0f63d958136789ad1fe3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27920" type="x-p"/> The weld beasts of the desert - ציים tsiyim, the mountain cats. - Bochart. <div eID="gen27920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27921" type="x-p"/> Wild beasts of the island - איים aiyim, the jackals. <div eID="gen27921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27922" type="x-p"/> The satyr - שעיר seir, the hairy one, probably the he-goat. <div eID="gen27922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27923" type="x-p"/> The screech owl - לילית lilith, the night-bird, the night-raven, nyctycorax, from ליל layil, or לילה lailah, the night.
entries.e139507e9bb7efc508ca6b37314733c24905c722: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27924" type="x-p"/> The great owl - קפוז kippoz, the ακοντιας, or darter, a serpent so called because of its suddenly leaping up or darting on its prey. Probably the mongoose or ichneumon may be intended. <div eID="gen27924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27925" type="x-p"/> The vultures - דיות daiyoth, the black vultures. My old MS. Bible renders these names curiously: And ageyn cumen schul devylis: the beste, party of an asse, and party of a mam: and the wodwose, the tother schal crien to the tother. There schal byn lamya, that is, thrisse, or a beste, havynge the body liic a woman, and hors feet. Ther hadde dichis, the yrchoun, and nurshide out littil chittis. There ben gadred kiitis, the top to the top. What language! <div eID="gen27925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27926" type="x-p"/> Every one with her mate - A MS. adds אל el after אשה ishshah, which seems necessary to the construction; and so the Syriac and Vulgate. Another MS. adds in the same place את eth, which is equivalent.
entries.77bbadb5228d94886017eb84d9a18531843f3704: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen27926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27927" type="x-p"/> My mouth "For the mouth of Jehovah" - For הוא hu, five MSS., (three ancient), read יהוה Jehovah, and another is so corrected; so likewise the Septuagint. Two editions have צום tsivam; and so the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic, with the edition of 1486, and a MS. has קבצם kebatsam, with the masculine pronoun instead of the feminine: and so in the next verses it is להם lahem, instead of להן lahen, in fourteen MSS., six of them ancient. - L. To see the importance of these various readings, the Hebrew Bible must be consulted.  <chapter eID="Isa.34"/> <div eID="gen27927" type="x-p"/>

entries.23e63e8b66ce41934218a7a96c3f8a8891412e83: <reference osisRef="Isa.34.1-Isa.34.3">Isa 34:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13232" type="x-p"/> What the prophet here foretells relates to all nations, and to every individual within them, in their relation to the congregation of Jehovah. He therefore commences with the appeal in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.1-Isa.34.3">Isa 34:1-3</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Come near, ye peoples, to hear; and he nations, attend. Let the earth hear, and that which fills it, the world, and everything that springs from it. For the indignation of Jehovah will fall upon all nations, and burning wrath upon all their host; He has laid the ban upon them, delivered them to the slaughter. And their slain are cast away, and their corpses - their stench will arise, and mountains melt with their blood.”</hi> The summons does not invite them to look upon the completion of the judgment, but to hear the prophecy of the future judgment; and it is issued to everything on the earth, because it would all have to endure the judgment upon the nations (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.10">Isa 13:10</reference>). The expression <hi type="italic">qetseph layehōvâh</hi> implies that Jehovah was ready to execute His wrath (compare <hi type="italic">yōm layehōvâh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.8">Isa 34:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.2.12">Isa 2:12</reference>). The nations that are hostile to Jehovah are slaughtered, the bodies remain unburied, and the streams of blood loosen the firm masses of the mountains, so that they melt away. On the stench of the corpses, compare Eze 39:11. Even if <hi type="italic">châsam</hi>, in this instance, does not mean “to take away the breath with the stench,” there is no doubt that Ezekiel had this prophecy of Isaiah in his mind, when prophesying of the destruction of Gog and Magog (Ezek 39).
entries.b45a554d68bb0ec57ceb14633e8f82f97dd09327: <reference osisRef="Isa.34.4">Isa 34:4</reference> <div eID="gen13232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13233" type="x-p"/> The judgment foretold by Isaiah also belongs to the last things; for it takes place in connection with the simultaneous destruction of the present heaven and the present earth.<hi type="italic">”And all the host of the heavens moulder away, and the heavens are rolled up like a scroll, and all their host withers as a leaf withers away from the vine, and like withered leaves from the fig-tree”</hi> (<hi type="italic">Nâmaq</hi>, to be dissolved into powdered mother (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.24">Isa 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>); <hi type="italic">nâgōl</hi> (for <hi type="italic">nâgal</hi>, like <hi type="italic">nâzōl</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.63.19">Isa 63:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.2">Isa 64:2</reference>, and <hi type="italic">nârōts</hi> in <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.6">Ecc 12:6</reference>), to be rolled up - a term applied to the cylindrical book-scroll. The heaven, that is to say, the present system of the universe, breaks up into atoms, and is rolled up like a book that has been read through; and the stars fall down as a withered leaf falls from a vine, when it is moved by even the lightest breeze, or like the withered leaves shaken from the fig-tree. The expressions are so strong, that they cannot be understood in any other sense than as relating to the end of the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa 65:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.22">Isa 66:22</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">Mat 24:29</reference>). It is not sufficient to say that “the stars appear to fall to the earth,” though even Vitringa gives this explanation. <div eID="gen13233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13234" type="x-p"/> When we look, however, at the following <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi> (for), it undoubtedly appears strange that the prophet should foretell the passing away of the heavens, simply because Jehovah judges Edom. But Edom stands here as the representative of all powers that are hostile to the church of God as such, and therefore expresses an idea of the deepest and widest cosmical signification (as <reference osisRef="Isa.24.21">Isa 24:21</reference> clearly shows). And it is not only a doctrine of Isaiah himself, but a biblical doctrine universally, that God will destroy the present world as soon as the measure of the sin which culminates in unbelief, and in the persecution of the congregation of the faithful, shall be really full.
entries.105e4a70b7418a8d56f645c4f2a36016b7657844: <reference osisRef="Isa.34.5-Isa.34.7">Isa 34:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen13234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13235" type="x-p"/> If we bear this in mind, we shall not be surprised that the prophet gives the following reason for the passing away of the present heavens. <hi type="italic">“For my sword has become intoxicated in the heaven; behold, it comes down upon Edom, and upon the people of my ban to judgment. The sword of Jehovah fills itself with blood, is fattened with fat, with blood of lambs and he-goats, with kidney-fat of rams; for Jehovah has a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom. And buffaloes fall with them, and bullocks together with bulls; and their land become intoxicated with blood, and their dust fattened with fat.”</hi> Just as in chapter 63 Jehovah is represented as a treader of the wine-press, and the nations as the grapes; so here He is represented as offering sacrifice, and the nations as the animals offered (<hi type="italic">zebhach</hi>: cf., Zep 1:7; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">Jer 46:10</reference>); Eze 39:17.: all three passages founded upon this). Jehovah does not appear here in person as judge, as He does there, but His sword appears; just as in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen 3:24</reference>, the “sword which turned every way” is mentioned as an independent power standing by the side of the cherub. The sword is His executioner, which has no sooner drunk deeply of wrath <hi type="italic">in heaven</hi>, i.e., in the immediate sphere of the Deity (<hi type="italic">rivvethâh</hi>, an intensive form of the <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, like <hi type="italic">pittēăch</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa 48:8</reference>; Ewald, §120,<hi type="italic">d</hi>), than it comes down in wild intoxication upon Edom, the people of the ban of Jehovah, i.e., the people upon whom He has laid the ban, and there, as His instrument of punishment, fills itself with blood, and fattens itself with fat. הדּשׁנה is the <hi type="italic">hothpaal</hi> = התדּשׁנה, with the ת of the preformative syllable assimilated (compare הזּכּוּ in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16">Isa 1:16</reference>, and אדּמּה in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.14">Isa 14:14</reference>). The penultimate has the tone, the <hi type="italic">nâh</hi> being treated as in the plural forms of the future. The dropping of the <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> in the שׁ eht ni hse is connected with this. The reading מחלב, in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Isa 34:6</reference>, is an error that has been handed down in modern copies (in opposition to both codices and ancient editions); for חלב (primary form, <hi type="italic">chilb</hi>) is the only form met with in the Old Testament. The lambs, he-goats, and rams, represent the Edomitish nation, which is compared to these smaller sacrificial animals. <hi type="italic">Edom</hi> and <hi type="italic">Bozrah</hi> are also placed side by side in Isa 63:1. The latter was one of the chief cities of the Edomites (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.33">Gen 36:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.12">Amo 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.13">Jer 49:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference>) - not the Bozrah in Auranitis (<hi type="italic">Haurân</hi>), however, which is well known in church history, but Bozrah in the mountains of Edom, upon the same site as the village of <hi type="italic">Buzaire</hi> (i.e., Minor Bozrah), which is still surrounded by its ruins. In contrast with the three names of the smaller animals in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Isa 34:6</reference>, the three names of oxen in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.7">Isa 34:7</reference> represent the lords of Edom. They also will fall, smitten by the sword (<hi type="italic">yâredū</hi>: cf., <reference osisRef="Jer.50.27">Jer 50:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.40">Jer 51:40</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Jer.48.15">Jer 48:15</reference>). The feast of the sword is so abundant, that even the earth and the dust of the land of Edom are satiated with blood and fat.
entries.f327ae9a985266e87e89059d89b64d06f3c92e6c: <reference osisRef="Isa.34.8-Isa.34.10">Isa 34:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen13235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13236" type="x-p"/> Thus does Jehovah avenge His church upon Edom. <hi type="italic">“For Jehovah hath a day of vengeance, a year of recompense, to contend for Zion. And the brooks of Edom are turned into pitch, and its dust into brimstone, and its land becomes burning pitch. Day and night it is not quenched; the smoke of Edom goes up for ever: it lies waste from generation to generation; no one passes through it for ever and ever.”</hi> The one expression, “to contend for Zion,” is like a flash of lightning, throwing light upon the obscurity of prophecy, both backwards and forwards. A day and a year of judgment upon Edom (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.61.2">Isa 61:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.4">Isa 63:4</reference>) would do justice to Zion against its accusers and persecutors (<hi type="italic">rı̄bh</hi>, <hi type="italic">vindicare</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.51.22">Isa 51:22</reference>). The everlasting punishment which would fall upon it is depicted in figures and colours, suggested by the proximity of Edom to the Dead Sea, and the volcanic character of this mountainous country. The unquenchable fire (for which compare <reference osisRef="Isa.66.24">Isa 66:24</reference>), and the eternally ascending smoke (cf., <reference osisRef="Rev.19.3">Rev 19:3</reference>), prove that the end of all things is referred to. The prophet meant primarily, no doubt, that the punishment announced would fall upon the land of Edom, and within its geographical boundaries; but this particular punishment represented the punishment of all nations, and all men who were Edomitish in their feelings and conduct towards the congregation of Jehovah.
